newsitem.title: UK: British Lockerbie relatives get compensation offer.
newsitem.headline: British Lockerbie relatives get compensation offer.

text.p: Relatives of British victims of the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am jet over Scotland are set to accept a final improved offer of compensation which press reports said on Wednesday would be about 500,000 pounds ($826,300) each.
Lawyer Peter Watson, who represents the families, said he hoped to make an announcement about the compensation offer in about a week.

"As far as the Lockerbie Disaster Group is concerned, this is the end of the matter," Watson told Reuters. Watson said the offer had been made by USIR, the United States aviation underwriters, acting as Pan Am's insurers.
Pan Am, which collapsed in debt in 1991, weakened after the bombing over Lockerbie and stiff industry competition. It was relaunched as a smaller company, Pan Am World Airways Inc, in September.

"An offer has been made through me and passed to the families to be considered," Watson said, but declined to reveal the sums involved. "A lot of paperwork is still to be done but I hope to be able to make an announcement in about a week."
Of the 270 people killed in the December 1988 bombing, 33 were British passengers on the Pan Am jumbo, and 11 were residents in the village of Lockerbie where the jet crashed.
In 1992, a jury in New York ruled Pan Am was responsible for allowing the bomb on board the flight. Since then, families of the victims have been fighting for compensation.

Pamela Dix, secretary of the U.K. Families Flight 103 group representing the British victims, said settlement was very close. "It is in its last stages," said Dix, whose brother Peter was on the Pan Am flight.
"People will be happy to put this aspect of the disaster behind them. It has been a protracted exercise, there will be a sense of relief," Dix said.

She told Reuters some British families had settled for unspecified amounts before the latest offer. "Each case is individual, entirely separate," she told Reuters. The families of the American victims have already received an estimated $500 million in damages from Pan Am's insurers.

If the British families accept the latest offer, it would close the civil side of legal proceedings surrounding the bombing, although the criminal side is far from settled. Warrants were issued in 1992 for the arrest of Libyans Abdel Basset Mohammed Al-Megrahi and Al-Amin Khalifa Fhimah, suspected by the United States and Britain for their part in bombing.
The two men have refused to stand trial in Scotland or the United States, saying they will not get a fair trial.

Sanctions were imposed on Libya because Colonel Muammar Gaddafi refused to hand the men, over for trial. Lawyers for the suspects said their clients were ready to sit before a Scottish judge, using Scottish law, at a tribunal in a neutral country. ($1=.6051 Pound)
